speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: First, the top marginal personal income tax (PIT), rate of tax-resident individuals will be increased from the Year of Assessment 2024.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: The PIT rates for certain income by non-tax-resident individuals that are pegged to the top marginal tax rate of tax-resident individuals will also be revised to 24%.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Clauses 22, 42 and 44 of the Bill provide for these amendments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Second, to support data-driven policy-making, operations and integrated service delivery, we propose two amendments to the Income Tax Act and Goods and Services Tax Act to facilitate the disclosure of information by the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) for official duties.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: The first change relates to the scenario where taxpayers such as individuals and companies have provided consent for their information to be shared.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Today, IRAS can disclose such information to public sector agencies or an authorised person who is engaged by the Government or a Statutory Board, if the disclosure is for the sole purpose of administering a written law or public scheme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: For example, to determine what level of subsidy a patient can receive, healthcare personnel in hospitals designated to administer public healthcare schemes may obtain such information with consent, to provide the appropriate subsidies to patients efficiently and conveniently.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: However, the current approach has some limitations where the official duties of public officers go beyond administering written law or a public scheme – such as for policy-making or providing public services in an integrated manner.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: For example, Enterprise Singapore needs to regularly review its internationalisation schemes that support local companies expanding into overseas markets.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Even if the companies have given consent for their information to be shared with Enterprise Singapore, IRAS is currently unable to do so, because such a review does not fall under “administration of a written law or public scheme”.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Where taxpayers have provided consent for IRAS to disclose their information to a public officer, or an authorised person outside the public sector who is engaged by the Government or a Statutory Board, the proposed amendment in the Bill will enable such disclosure by IRAS for the performance of official duties.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: This will apply only to company-related information and does not include data of individuals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: This list of company-related information will be prescribed in the Income Tax Act and Goods and Services Tax Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: With access to the data on specific companies, a public sector agency will be able to identify which are the companies that could benefit from certain enterprise development schemes and proactively share with them information on the relevant schemes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Without the data sharing, we are faced with a chicken-and-egg problem.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: These companies may miss out on the benefits as they do not know that they are eligible and they may not apply for the schemes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: We recognise that this approach can be sensitive and we need to strike a balance between improving service efficiency and convenience, versus protecting data confidentiality.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: First, information in the prescribed list will be provided in a less granular form.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: For instance, the company’s sales revenue will be shared in ranges, rather than the exact value.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Such information will also not be disclosed to any person outside the public sector, even if the person is engaged by the Government or a Statutory Board.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: It will only be disclosed to public officers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Clauses 3, 41, 43, 46 and 49 of the Bill provide for these amendments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: The information on taxpayers will continue to be safeguarded under existing tax legislation, the Official Secrets Act and the Public Sector (Governance) Act, as well as data governance policies set out in the Government’s Instruction Manuals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Collectively, these data protections set out when data can be shared across agencies, limit the access to data to only authorised persons and ensure accountability for access and use of data through penalties for unauthorised disclosure and improper use of data.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: All persons with access to such information on taxpayers are bounded by secrecy provisions under the applicable tax legislation – Income Tax Act or Goods and Services Tax Act – and the Official Secrets Act, where any unauthorised disclosure of such data is an offence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Where personal data is involved, non-Government Entities acting on behalf of the Government will also be subject to the Personal Data Protection Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: First, we will update the definition of local employee for the Mergers and Acquisitions Scheme, to recognise individuals hired under central hiring and secondment arrangements as employees of the acquiring company.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Currently, only individuals that are directly hired by the acquiring company are taken into account for assessing whether the three local employee condition is met.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: As businesses may have different hiring practices, the change allows us greater flexibility to recognize an equivalent material outcome of local workers being hired, be it through direct hiring, central hiring, or secondment arrangements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Clause 21 of the Bill provides for this amendment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Currently, each hearing committee comprises at least three BOR members.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: In deciding whether or not to convene a one-member coram, the chairperson will consider the parties’ submissions, as well as the facts and circumstances of the case.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Taken together, these changes will allow greater flexibility and ensure that BOR cases are resolved in a more timely and efficient manner.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Related amendments will also be made to the BOR provisions in the Goods and Services Tax Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Clauses 34, 35, 36, 37, 38 and 46 of the Bill provide for these amendments.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: My speech, in particular, will focus on the amendments to facilitate the sharing of information by IRAS for official duties.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Under the current section 6 (Official Secrecy) of both Income Tax Act (ITA) and Goods and Services Tax Act (GSTA), IRAS is obliged to preserve the confidentiality of a taxpayer’s information unless it is for the administration of any written law or public scheme.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Better and judicious use of data can significantly improve the effectiveness of Government, operations and also better service to the public.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: However, the obvious concern is how do we safeguard taxpayers’ confidentiality; especially where IRAS may be privy to documents containing sensitive commercial information.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In this regard, I have a few questions for the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: First, whether the agencies requesting the information from IRAS would need to justify the specific purposes and use of the information?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: What is the governance and accountability structure here?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Thirdly, would the changes have any impact our competitiveness as a premier destination to attract international investments, now that we can disclose this information to the agencies?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Fourthly, with this expansion of the scope for data disclosures and sharing, would there be further safeguards to ensure data confidentiality and privacy?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is on this basis of high public trust and integrity that we can then look to further harnessing the value of data within the public sector system to provide more effective government and better public service.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, I will concentrate my remarks on clause 46, which concerns related amendments to the Goods and Services Tax Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My speech will focus on the general merits and principles behind these amendments and, in particular, the impending increase in GST, which in part, necessitates these amendments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: More specifically, I wish to revisit the case for rebating fiscal surpluses, in lieu of a more immediate in GST.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As Members of this House are aware, consumer prices continued their stubborn climb in August.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Pause for a moment and consider what this implies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Were inflation to remain at this rate, prices would double in just nine years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Think – in 2031, a plate of chicken rice, my favourite example, will cost $7 instead of $3.50.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A slightly used Honda Civic would be $220,000 and that is assuming COE prices do not increase further.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A four-room BTO flat in Sengkang, the constituency I represent, would go for $700,000 and likely double that in the resale market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To place this number in even more stark context, for the half decade between 2016 and 2021, median household income rose by a respectable 2.8% per annum, after adjusting for inflation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But had inflation been just at rates experienced over the past six months, paychecks would have shrunk by about half that rate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For those of us that still rent, the hit has been even more severe.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Stories of landlords raising rental by up to 40% are not unheard of.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This means that, much like in the US and a number of other economies, price rises are gradually becoming entrenched in people's expectations, running the risk of a self-reinforcing inflation cycle.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I do not expect inflation to remain at an elevated level of more than 7% over the next decade, nor do I expect that the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) does either.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But that does not detract from the fact that higher prices have significantly eroded the purchasing power of Singaporean families.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That real and present danger of inflation becoming persistent means that the monetary authority cannot simply stand pat in the face of price pressures.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It has already adjusted depreciation path of the Singapore dollar four times over the past year and has even taken on a more aggressive stance of adjusting the exchange rate upward over the past two cycles.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is concern that in a small, export-oriented economy, an excessively strong Singapore dollar will erode our competitiveness.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Since October of last year, Singapore's exchange rate relative to its main trading partners has appreciated by almost 5%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even so, the main bilateral rate of interest, the dollar exchange rate between Singapore and the US, for which global commodities such as agriculture and energy which we import are pegged, has gone the other way and depreciated by close to 6%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Small wonder then, that in our economy, which is almost entirely reliant on imported food and fuel, we have continued to battle under the weight of inflation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Singapore's inflation dynamics appear to closely track that of the US, writ small.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And since the Federal Reserve remains undeterred in its effort to raise interest rates to break the back of domestic inflation in the US, it is not unreasonable to expect for MAS to embark on at least another round of tightening monetary policy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Things look to remain challenging at least a while longer before they get any better.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, it appears increasingly likely that we may need to accept that a soft landing, that our economy, where labour markets remain robust, may be a pipe dream.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And we if accept that unemployment has to rise, then, our workers are due for a double whammy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Singaporeans everywhere are already feeling the pinch from increases in the cost of living, hurting from things they were previously able to comfortably afford.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But should the economy be slow in response to tighter monetary policy, it is the marginal worker that will be displaced from their jobs, losing their incomes at a time when they least can afford it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: With the economy about to face a right jab and a left hook, do we really want to "shoryuken" our workers with a jump in prices of another 1% because of the GST rate hike in January?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, as I shared in my Adjournment Motion with this House on 5 July, we should not be building up fiscal surpluses at a time when the economy is still in recovery and inflation is biting into our citizens' pocketbooks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I suggested that instead, any excess revenues from taxes and duties should, as much as possible, be rebated back to our people.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is because fiscal policy should be playing a stabilising role rather than amplify the stresses felt by the private sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This increase was led by corporate income but individual tax receipts also rose as the revenue across the board for most sources.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The largest increase of $2.9 billion was due to higher stamp duties, which due to, in IRAS' own words, "a buoyant property market" and "an increase in property transactions".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Notably, the take from GST, also increased by 22% even without any increase in the rate of GST, telling me observers also expect the tax revenues in the upcoming fiscal year are likely to increase yet further.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One analyst said that he expected Government revenue to continue exceeding Budget projections while another believes that this increase will be due to strong corporate profits, rising wage growth and higher property tax and stamp duties.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In my speech on the Budget this year, I suggest that with the inflation fire burning as hot as it did, raising GST would only add fuel to the flame.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That was back in February, when inflation was only 4.3%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Government has previously argued that they stand ready to address inflation with additional measures.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong assured this House during his Budget speech and I quote: "If inflation turns out to be persistent and higher than expected, we as the Government will deal with this separately through other tools".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: He reiterated this position in April stating that the Government will assess the overall situation and then consider what additional steps they could take.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Whichever our base year, it is evident that last year's revenue was an anomaly larger than previously anticipated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another objection is that unexpectedly high surpluses, much of which are derived from real estate related duties, are unlikely to be replicated and hence should not be utilised for recurrent expenditure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We should not be planning recurring expenditures on the basis of one-off revenue gains.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet, what is being proposed here is likewise a one-off expenditure meant to tide households over this difficult period of high inflation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Nobody expects a continuous stream of payout from the Government once inflation returns to historical norms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, there is the prospect of even more extraordinary revenues in the forthcoming months.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This Government had previously indicated that it would be unwise to plan for new revenues arising from the OECD-led BEPS collaboration to roll out a minimum corporate tax.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This caution may appear to be warranted, given the unwillingness of the United States Congress to ratify the deal, which ironically, it helped broker.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But Mark Twain, the American novelist and social critic, is often said to have quipped that reports of his own death had been largely exaggerated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And much like this quote, reports of the demise of the global corporate minimum tax appear to be incorrect or at least premature.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There are good reasons to believe that in the medium run, there are strong incentives for non-adopters of the treaty, such as the US, to continue to do so, as long as other major economies also ratify it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The probability that this tax will proceed regardless of American participation or acquiescence lends further reason for the Government to rebate surplus tax revenue now.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Were the agreement to proceed, even in slightly diluted form, it will almost certainly require changes to local corporate tax laws that are far more likely to raise corporate tax revenues then diminish them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The takeaway is that we appear to have fiscal wiggle room to move forward with such a rebate, both now and in the future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What are some options that may be available to the Government should it choose to rebate the $8.7 million windfall revenue?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One approach is to postpone the GST tax increases.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even if we accept that we cannot, in Deputy Prime Minister Wong's own words, "keep delaying the GST tax increase given our pressing revenue needs", we can at least try to forestall the increase for another two years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This will afford our households and businesses a breather and allow our economy to avoid a simultaneous constriction of both monetary and fiscal policy next year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another alternative is to distribute the amount via GST Vouchers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This will amount to another beefing up of the GST Voucher scheme similar to what had been announced earlier this year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Government had previously suggested that GST expenses would be fully offset for almost 20 years for our poorest households and even for the richest, they will be covered for around two and a half years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another GST Voucher distribution with a for temporary targeted and timely support for our most vulnerable groups and help restore the Government's original promise of the number of years of offset.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A third strategy is to roll another off-Budget support package that would offer broad support, similar to the Resilience, Solidarity, Fortitude and Assurance packages, for which I am sure, the Government will accompany with another clever moniker – perhaps "Reassurance".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such a move recognises not only lower-income quintile groups, while undeniably disproportionately affected by inflation, are not the only ones that have faced difficulties due to a higher cost of living.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, the Government may choose as it did during this year's Budget to combine a broad package that is with additional GST Voucher support.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These private individuals have to execute a declaration of secrecy and commit an offence if they were to disclose such information received.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the Minister tell us what is the penalty involved for this offence?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is more severe than the penalty under the Income Tax Act and yet, income information is something that most consider highly confidential and sensitive, more so than other personal data, like addresses, phone numbers and so on.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will the Minister review the penalty for unauthorised disclosure of income information?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What penalties are in place for unauthorised utilisation of information?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The financial gains for such unauthorised utilisation may outweigh a $5,000 fine.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Bill also permits the Comptroller to disclose information listed in the 11th Schedule without the person's consent.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I had earlier intended to ask for an explanation of under what circumstances this would be required.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But I note from the Senior Minister of State's speech earlier that he mentioned that this is for the purpose of certain Government departments being able to proactively approach companies that may qualify for certain Government financial assistance or other assistance programmes.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I appreciate the good intention of this move but feel that it would be better if the Bill then specifies under what circumstances such disclosure without consent can take place, instead of leaving it open-ended, which then throws the gate open for disclosure without consent under any other circumstances.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The 11th Schedule currently lists only company information and not information on individuals.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, clause 41 of the Bill allows the Minister to amend the 11th Schedule.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This seems to suggest that the Minister will be able to add personal information into the 11th Schedule subsequently.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If so, this would raise privacy concerns and is quite a major departure from what the current Bill contains.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have grave concerns about this power being vested in a single individual.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I therefore suggest that instead of amending section 106(3), to insert instead section 106(4) to allow the Minister to amend the 11th Schedule subject to the barring of any individual information being included.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On the whole, these changes will make our tax system fairer and more efficient, and support Singapore's growth across a whole slew of sectors.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on information sharing by IRAS.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, can the Senior Minister of State share in what situations do Government bodies envision using the information-sharing provisions in the new section 6(12)?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, can	the Senior Minister of State share how will IRAS obtain "express consent" under the new section 6(12)?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When seeking consent, to what standards will the Government bodies hold themselves?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will they state the exact piece of information to be shared, the frequency of this information sharing, the recipient of the information and the intended usage of that information?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Or will Government bodies ask for a blanket agreement without providing such details?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Third, can	the Senior Minister of State share if someone can be held in contempt of the authority of a public servant for not providing consent to disclose their income information under section 6(12)?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: After all, many actions involving non-disclosure of information constitute such an offence under the Penal Code, including refusal to answer a public servant authorised to question and obstructing a public servant in discharge of their public functions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One piece of information is whether a company claimed deductions under seven sections in the Income Tax Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can	the Senior Minister of State share why these seven specific sections were chosen for the 11th Schedule?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Why not any of the other deductions in Part 5 of the Act?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The rationale for the differentiated treatment is unclear.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second area of clarifications is on the hearing of appeals by the Board of Review.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The chairperson is required to have regard to the facts and circumstances of a case in deciding whether to appoint only a single member to hear the case.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State share if the chairperson will take into account the preferences of the parties to the case in deciding whether a hearing by a single Board member is appropriate?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, there may be cases where the issues are not complex but the relationship between parties are extremely acrimonious and it may be preferable to have the case heard by a panel.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, the Bill proposes substituting a number of terms.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State clarify if these substitutions are intended to be significant?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, "in the absence of a member of Board" is substituted by "by committee where a member becomes unavailable".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Additionally, "do not consent" is substituted by "object" in a number of provisions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Is this substitution significant and is a positive expression of an objection now required where previously the absence of consent would suffice?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Third, sections 80A and 80B allow parties to object to the hearing of an appeal in various cases.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Section 80A provides that "the parties may object" whereas section 80B provides that "any party may object".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State clarify if the objection of a single party is sufficient in both cases?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If not, can the Senior Minister of State clarify when are the objections of both parties required and what is the rationale for drawing this distinction?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Since the 1980s, it has been amended almost every year so as to carry out the Government's revised fiscal strategy announced in its latest Budget Statement.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many of the matters of policy or principle would already have been debated in this House when the Government's 2022 Budget Statement was presented.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hence, I would just like to seek some clarifications on the specific changes proposed in this amendment Bill, before touching on a couple of issues which I believe should be considered in our periodic review of Singapore's income tax system.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In Malay):   This amendment Bill does not seek to implement all the tax changes announced by the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance at Budget 2022.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: By my calculation, this change will only affect individuals who are making an average of more than $41,000 per month.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister has commented during the Budget debate that we cannot sustain a tax system and hold our society together if "the bulk or all of the tax burden is borne by a small group of people at the top end".

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Based on current data, may I ask how many taxpayers will this change affect?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What proportion of the total personal income tax collected are they already responsible for today?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Since the announcement of such an increase in February 2022, has the Government or IRAS detected any efforts by such high-income individuals to "offshore" their earnings?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am concerned that the lead-time before 2024 would allow companies and individuals to restructure their remuneration packages and erode the additional revenue we expect to receive.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In English): Moving on to my second area of focus.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Of particular interest to me are the amendments to facilitate disclosure of tax information to support data-driven policy-making, operations and integrated service delivery.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Just this year, I have spoken in this House and filed a Parliamentary Question on how we should leverage data and technology to "push" schemes and services to Singaporeans and Singaporean businesses.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The amendment Bill broadens the powers of the Comptroller of Income Tax to disclose tax information to any public officer or officer of a statutory board for the performance of any official duties, in some cases without the consent of the person to whom the information relates.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We have already seen how useful such tax information can be.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, there is no doubt that the tax information is highly sensitive and confidential.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If we are to expect an increased flow of such information between Ministries and Statutory Boards, will there be any enhanced safeguards to protect the secrecy of the data?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The SingHealth episode tells us that the risks of cyberattacks and data breaches cannot be understated.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Government data is not immune from these risks.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In fact, they are likely to be higher value targets for malicious threats.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What percentage of taxpayers have already provided their express consent to the existing disclosure regime and how does the Government or IRAS intend to obtain fresh consent for the new, expanded disclosure regime?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Has there been any public consultations with companies which may be impacted and the extent of data which may be disclosed without consent and what the data collected will be used for?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I believe the Senior Minister of State has given a brief explanation on what the data will be used for, but I think my other questions are somewhat new in some ways.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The third area in my speech is something that relates to the administrative flexibility that characterises the Government.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As I understand it, clause 15 of the amendment Bill seeks to harmonise the accounting basis on which insurance companies prepare their financial statements.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Insurance companies will no longer have to prepare financial statements on one basis for the purpose of regulatory returns to be submitted to the MAS and another set of financial statements on a different accounting basis for tax computation purposes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Even though this change may cause IRAS to have to deal with insurance companies on a different reporting cycle from other taxpayers, I expect such a change to help reduce compliance costs for tax-paying insurance companies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In turn, this could further improve their profitability in the longer term, leading to an increase in the corporate income tax collected.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can this be extended more generally to other types of companies as well?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Taken together with the move to facilitate the disclosure and flow of tax information between Ministries and Statutory Boards, there may even be room for companies to file a single return to satisfy all its regulatory tax and other statutory obligations in future.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This may not be a simple switch, but I urge the Government to consider such a possibility as it would boost Singapore's attractiveness as a place for doing business.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My fourth area of focus relates to the changes to the appeal process before the Income Tax Board of Review.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will different fees be prescribed for appeals before a one-person panel and before a three-person panel?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will the factors guiding the chairperson's discretion be set out in regulations?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Because section 80(2) presently states that an appellant can attend "in person" but that will be removed under clause 36 of the amendment Bill.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As I had again raised in my speech during the Budget debate this year, it may be useful to relook the option of assessing personal income tax on a current-year, pay-as-you-earn basis.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the current economic environment, individuals may experience volatility in income levels or in employment from one year to the next.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Please allow me to now respond to the points they have raised.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked how many taxpayers will be affected by the increase in the top marginal personal income tax, or PIT, rate, the proportion of the total PIT contributed by them and our projections of additional revenue which can be collected.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat also asked whether the Government or IRAS has detected any attempts by high income individuals to "offshore" their earnings, such as restructuring or moving their assets overseas to avoid tax in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This includes instances where individuals derive income from providing services in Singapore to overseas-based employers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: They are subject to income tax in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We do not tax individuals on foreign-sourced income.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For example, a person who acquires income generating assets overseas such as by investing in overseas property will pay the applicable taxes and other costs in that jurisdiction.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: IRAS has a robust compliance and audit programme to identify high risk cases for review.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Members are aware that we have been raising our taxes for higher-income individuals in recent years such that those who earn more contribute more.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As Mr Saktiandi Supaat alluded to in his question, many high net worth individuals are globally mobile and some of them may shift away from Singapore to alternative jurisdictions with more competitive tax rates if our tax rates are too high.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If this happens, our tax base and our tax collections will be eroded.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We therefore need to weigh the trade-offs carefully.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat suggested that PIT could be assessed on a current year, pay-as-you-earn basis so that taxpayers can better manage their cashflow by matching tax payments with current year income.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is an alternative that we considered before and there are pros and cons to adopting such an approach.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: First, a current year, pay-as-you-earn basis for PIT assessment means that the tax payable will be withheld every month by employers and then paid to IRAS.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: While it matches tax payments more closely with the taxpayer's income, it also reduces their take home pay every month instead of giving them the option of paying the tax using their annual bonus or other sources of income.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Second, some individuals, especially self-employed persons and those with higher variable salary components, may have difficulties estimating their current year income for tax reporting purposes.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Third, such a system could result in greater compliance cost for taxpayers and higher administration costs for IRAS compared to the current arrangement where individuals pay their taxes this year based on actual income earned in the previous year.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: To help taxpayers with their cashflow, which I think is the intent of what Mr Saktiandi's suggestion is about, IRAS allows interest-free GIRO instalments up to 12 months for individuals and 10 months for companies.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For those who have difficulties paying, sometimes due to unforeseen personal and family circumstances, they can approach IRAS for assistance.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: During the economic downturn such as in 2020, we automatically deferred GIRO deductions for corporate tax and income tax for self-employed persons to help them manage their cashflows.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Saktiandi also asked if we could extend the approach taken to ease insurance companies' tax filing compliance by harmonising the accounting basis, to other general taxpayers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I wish to clarify that insurance companies, like any other company, are not required to prepare a separate set of financial statements for tax purposes.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Companies use the information in their financial statements primarily to prepare their tax computations.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Due to changes in the financial reporting standard for insurance contracts, the financial statements of insurance companies will no longer include some information needed to prepare their tax computations.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will allow insurance companies to use the relevant information in the regulatory returns filed with MAS for tax computation purposes.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There were some one-off upsides that we got this year	– I think he acknowledged those points as well	– from property, for example.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But the overall fiscal space for Singapore remains tight, especially because, looking ahead, we also have some structural changes in our society, such as an ageing population which will require us to spend more on healthcare.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This has been explained previously by Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong and also, I believe, Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat when he was the Minister for Finance.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, yes, inflation is higher than when we first started but our assurance and our commitment remain that we will make sure that lower-income Singaporeans will not feel the impact of the increase in GST for at least 10 years.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Thirdly, on the impact of higher prices, the Deputy Prime Minister has also said in this House and also at other forums that the Government is monitoring closely what the impact of higher prices is on households and families, especially on lower- and middle-income households.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Because as I mentioned in my reply to Mr Ang Wei Neng earlier during Question Time, lower- and middle-income households face a bigger impact from rising prices.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Therefore, we want to make sure that we provide more help to these families.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There will be some schemes, as Assoc Prof Jamus Lim also acknowledged, that will be broad-based and would be helping every family like the CDC Vouchers and the Household Utilities Credit, but there will be some that are more targeted towards lower- and middle-income households.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Also, as we look ahead, how we can help our companies to transform, improve productivity, become more innovative, more competitive, help our workers, through our tripartite partnership with employers and with unions, to upskill and become more productive.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is still the most fundamental and most effective way of helping our workers to cope with rising inflation.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is to help them to increase their wages in a sustainable way through a combination of policies but also through skills upgrading, productivity improvements, making sure that Singapore's economy remains competitive.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If we can do that, then, as Assoc Prof Jamus Lim mentioned, we can then have real wage growth, real income growth.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: He gave some ideas of what could be done.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: These are actually very much in line with what the Government has already done.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Some of the existing measures – he mentioned GST Vouchers, he mentioned some of the support packages that we have, some of the rebates that we can give	– these are things that we have done.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said, we will continue to monitor the situation and if it is necessary to do so, we are prepared to provide more help, to help Singaporeans to cope with rising prices.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Different cases may bring up different factors and considerations.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The chairperson would be best placed to make a judgement call, taking into account the pertinent facts and circumstances in individual cases.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Louis Ng asked a related question on whether the chairperson will consider parties' preferences in deciding whether to appoint a single-member quorum.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The parties may indicate their preferences in their submissions and these inputs will be considered by the chairperson in making the decision.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: On the appearance by an appellant company before the Board of Review, the proposed new section 80(2) is intended to make clear that there is no need for physical hearings to be held.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It does not alter the existing position on who may appear before the board as an appellant company representative.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked if the substitutions of certain terms are intended to be significant, such as replacing "do not consent" with "object to" and replacing "in the absence of member of board" to "by committee where member becomes unavailable" in section 80A.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: They do not effect a change in the substantive meanings of the terms they replace.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Louis Ng also sought clarification on whether any difference is intended between sections 80A and 80B, as to whether the objection of a single party is sufficient or if such objections will have to be made by both parties.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The intention is the same for both sections.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Next, I will address the clarifications raised by Members on the proposed amendment to facilitate the disclosure of information by IRAS for official duties.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa sought clarifications on the evaluation process and governance for data sharing.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: IRAS evaluates each request for information against existing tax legislation as well as a standardised set of criteria set out in the Government's instruction manual.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This includes ensuring that the purpose of disclosure is aligned with what is allowed in legislation and that the information requested is proportionate and relevant to the purpose.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Louis Ng asked under what situations IRAS would share information with public sector agencies and authorised third parties with the consent of taxpayers under the amended section 6(12).

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Currently, with taxpayer's consent, IRAS is already allowed to disclose information to public sector agencies and authorised persons engaged by the Government or Statutory Board if the disclosure is for the sole purpose of administering a written law or public scheme.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked if it would constitute a contempt of authority for refusing to provide consent to the disclosure of information under this section.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Louis Ng and Mr Saktiandi Supaat sought clarifications on the process of seeking consent from taxpayers to share their information.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The agency seeking consent will provide sufficient information in any request for consent so that taxpayers can make an informed decision whether to give their consent or not.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For example, the taxpayer will be told upfront of the information to be disclosed, the purpose of sharing such information and the persons whom the information may be disclosed to.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Consent that had been provided by taxpayers for IRAS to disclose the information for a purpose under the ambit of "administering a written law or public scheme" will continue to be valid.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Should public sector agencies require that information for another purpose beyond administering written law or a public scheme in the future, fresh consent will be required.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This will need to be obtained under the new section 6(12) as amended by this Bill.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Louis Ng and Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked about the basis for the prescribed list in a proposed new section 6(12B), which can be shared by IRAS with public sector agencies without requiring taxpayers' consent for the disclosure.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As I explained in my speech earlier, we have taken a calibrated approach to safeguard information confidentiality.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, these information in the prescribed list will be disclosed in less granular format, in ranges or as a yes-or-no field, rather than the exact value.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Ms Hazel Poa observed that the prescribed list could potentially be expanded to allow sharing of information and I think she acknowledged the point that I made that it would only be for company-related information.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I want to assure Ms Poa that this will continue to be the case – the prescribed list will only be for company-related information.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Collectively, these proposed amendments are intended to facilitate efficient data-driven policy-making, operations and integrated service delivery for public sector agencies to serve the public more effectively.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I agree with Members on the need for robust safeguards even as we do so.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Information on taxpayers will continue to be safeguarded under existing tax legislation, the Official Secrets Act and the Public Sector Governance Act, as well as the data governance and security policies set out in the Government's Instruction Manuals.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Besides offences stated in the tax legislation, the Public Sector Governance Act further criminalises the acts of unauthorised disclosure of data, improper use of data and unauthorised re-identification of individuals from anonymised data.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Ms Hazel Poa asked about the adequacy of penalties for unlawful disclosure of information by an authorised third party engaged to assist public officers with their official duties.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For such unlawful disclosure, the offender could also be subject to penalties under the Official Secrets Act, Personal Data Protection Act or other relevant Acts.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, it is not only through the tax legislation but also through other Acts.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As Mr Saktiandi Supaat pointed out, there is a need to continually bolster our data security in the face of evolving threats.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The Government has been actively strengthening our data security regime to protect sensitive data and this is an important area of work as we become more digitally connected.
